flowers.name: ★ State Flower: California Poppy
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full entry.
flowers.description: California's iconic state flower — orange satin petals that close at night and in overcast weather. Blooms in great golden drifts across hillsides. Drought tolerant. Self-seeds prolifically.

flowers.name: California Poppy
flowers.wildlife: Pollen source for native bees. Goldfinches eat seeds.
flowers.description: The quintessential California wildflower — silky orange-gold petals open in sun and close at night. Colors range from pale yellow to deep orange. Self-seeds freely and naturalizes into stunning drifts. Drought tolerant once established. Grows statewide from sea level to 7,000ft.

flowers.name: Blue-Eyed Grass
flowers.wildlife: Attracts small native bees. Good butterfly nectar plant.
flowers.description: Not a true grass — a native iris relative with grass-like leaves bearing bright violet-blue star-shaped flowers with yellow centers. One of California's most charming small wildflowers. Naturalizes well in lawns and meadow gardens.

flowers.name: Clarkia (Farewell to Spring)
flowers.habitat: Dry hillsides, open woodland, chaparral edges
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for Clarkia bee (Diadasia), which collects pollen exclusively from Clarkia. Important for specialist bees.
flowers.description: Satiny pink to lavender four-petaled flowers with contrasting spots and ruffled edges. One of California's most beautiful native annuals. Blooms just as Mediterranean summer heat begins — heralding the 'farewell to spring.' Named for explorer William Clark.

flowers.name: California Buckwheat
flowers.habitat: Dry slopes, chaparral, coastal sage scrub
flowers.wildlife: Host for 150+ species of native bees. Critical for Acmon Blue, Square-spotted Blue, and Mormon Metalmark butterflies. Goldfinches eat seeds in fall.
flowers.description: Cream-white to pink flat-topped flower clusters on a drought-tolerant shrubby plant. Blooms for months. Essential habitat plant for chaparral ecosystems — supports more native bee species than almost any other California plant. Turns russet-orange in fall providing additional ornamental interest.

flowers.name: Western Columbine
flowers.habitat: Moist slopes, stream banks, forest openings
flowers.wildlife: Essential hummingbird nectar plant — the red color and backward-facing spurs are hummingbird adaptations. Also visited by long-tongued bumblebees.
flowers.description: Nodding red and yellow flowers with distinctive backward-sweeping spurs — the most beautiful of western columbines. Grows naturally in moist mountain slopes from Alaska to Baja. Hummingbirds probe the nectar spurs. Delicate fernlike foliage.

flowers.name: Sticky Monkeyflower
flowers.wildlife: Hummingbird nectar plant. Host for Variable Checkerspot butterfly.
flowers.description: Showy orange-yellow tubular flowers on an aromatic sticky shrub. One of the most adaptable California native plants — grows on rocky dry slopes, coastal bluffs, and chaparral. Blooms for many months. Sticky foliage deters browsing. Takes extreme drought.

flowers.name: Yarrow (Western)
flowers.wildlife: Supports 100+ insect species. Host for many moth and butterfly caterpillars. Beneficial insect magnet.
flowers.description: Flat-topped white flower clusters on feathery aromatic foliage. One of the most ecologically valuable wildflowers — supports an extraordinary diversity of native insects as both larval host and nectar source. Spreads by rhizomes. Drought tolerant once established.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Oregon Grape
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full entry.
flowers.description: Oregon's state flower — a drought-tolerant native shrub with glossy holly-like leaves and racemes of bright yellow flowers followed by dusty blue berries.

flowers.name: Oregon Grape
flowers.wildlife: Early nectar for queen bumblebees. Blue berries eaten by 30+ bird species including grouse, waxwings, and robins.
flowers.description: Bold glossy compound leaves like holly, bright yellow flower clusters in early spring, and clusters of dusty blue berries that make a tart jelly. Evergreen shrub that tolerates deep shade under conifers. One of the most versatile Pacific Northwest native plants.

flowers.name: Camas
flowers.habitat: Wet meadows, prairies, open woodland with seasonal moisture
flowers.wildlife: Major bumblebee and native bee forage. Historically the most important food plant for many Northwest Native peoples — the bulbs were a staple crop.
flowers.description: Spectacular sky-blue flower spikes rising from grassy meadows in spring. The blue of camas meadows was so dense early explorers mistook them for lakes. The starchy bulbs were a dietary cornerstone for tribes across the Northwest. Plant in areas with seasonal moisture. Naturalized meadows are breathtaking.

flowers.name: Red Flowering Currant
flowers.habitat: Open slopes, woodland edges, stream banks
flowers.wildlife: First major hummingbird nectar plant of spring. Also visited by early queen bumblebees. Blue-black berries eaten by many bird species.
flowers.description: One of the first and most spectacular spring bloomers — cascading clusters of deep rose-red flowers appear before leaves. Blooms just as rufous hummingbirds arrive from migration. Drought tolerant once established. A Pacific Northwest garden essential.

flowers.name: Farewell-to-Spring
flowers.habitat: Dry open slopes, sagebrush steppe, rocky ground
flowers.wildlife: Host for specialist Clarkia bee. Native bee pollen source.
flowers.description: Delicate four-petaled flowers in pink to lavender with deeply cleft petals giving a frilled appearance. Blooms in dry rocky ground as spring transitions to summer heat. Native annual that self-seeds reliably. Named by Lewis and Clark during the Corps of Discovery expedition.

flowers.name: Blue Flax (Lewis's Flax)
flowers.wildlife: Native bee pollen source. Seeds eaten by goldfinches and pine siskins.
flowers.description: Sky-blue five-petaled flowers on delicate wiry stems that sway in the breeze. Each flower lasts only one day but plants produce new blooms continuously. Named for Meriwether Lewis. Extremely drought tolerant. Naturalizes beautifully in dry gardens.

flowers.name: Fawn Lily
flowers.habitat: Moist woodland, grassy slopes under oaks
flowers.wildlife: Early spring bee forage. Ants disperse seeds (myrmecochory).
flowers.description: Nodding white flowers with reflexed petals marked with yellow and brown at the base. Mottled brown-green leaves like a fawn's spots. Blooms in moist woodland understory before canopy leafs out. Slow from seed — 5–7 years to bloom, but very long-lived once established.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Coast Rhododendron
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full entry.
flowers.description: Washington's state flower — a large native rhododendron with spectacular rose-pink flower trusses growing in Pacific coastal forests.

flowers.name: Coast Rhododendron
flowers.wildlife: Hummingbird and bumblebee nectar. Dense evergreen thickets provide critical wildlife cover.
flowers.description: Washington's largest native flowering shrub — enormous trusses of rose-pink flowers on a shrub reaching 20 feet in ideal conditions. Thrives in the shade and moisture of Pacific coastal forests. The defining floral element of Cascade and Olympic forest understories.

flowers.name: Bitterroot
flowers.habitat: Rocky slopes, gravelly soil, dry exposed ridges
flowers.wildlife: Native bee pollen source. Seeds dispersed by ants.
flowers.description: Extraordinarily beautiful multi-petaled pink flowers emerging directly from rocky ground in spring — the leaves have already died back by bloom time. The epitome of alpine resilience. Named for Meriwether Lewis. Can survive years of drought. Montana's state flower.

flowers.name: Pearly Everlasting
flowers.habitat: Open slopes, roadsides, disturbed ground, meadows
flowers.wildlife: Host plant for American Lady butterfly. Deer resist. Important late-season nectar source.
flowers.description: Clusters of papery white flowers with yellow centers on silver-woolly stems and leaves. Retains its form when dried — used in dried arrangements for centuries. Blooms in midsummer when many other flowers have finished. Self-seeds freely.

flowers.name: Streambank Lupine
flowers.wildlife: Host for Silvery Blue and other blue butterflies. Important nitrogen fixer in riparian systems.
flowers.description: Tall spikes of blue-purple pea flowers above palmate silvery leaves. Native lupines are the backbone of the Pacific Northwest wildflower meadow — fixing nitrogen, feeding butterflies, and creating spectacular blue drifts. Self-seeds in disturbed areas.

flowers.name: Chocolate Lily
flowers.habitat: Grassy slopes, rocky outcrops, open woodland
flowers.wildlife: Pollinated by beetles and flies attracted to carrion scent. Seeds dispersed by ants.
flowers.description: Unusual nodding bell-shaped flowers mottled in brown-purple and greenish-yellow — they smell faintly of skunk or chocolate. One of the most unusual and fascinating Pacific Northwest wildflowers. Deeply lobed star-shaped seedpods. Forms colonies slowly from bulblets.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Sagebrush (Flower)
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full entry.
flowers.description: Nevada's state flower — while best known as a shrub, big sagebrush produces tiny yellow flowers and defines the Great Basin landscape.

flowers.name: Big Sagebrush
flowers.habitat: Great Basin desert, high desert plains, mountain foothills
flowers.wildlife: Sage grouse depend on it year-round for food and cover. Pronghorn browse it in winter. Supports specialist insects.
flowers.description: The defining plant of the Great Basin — silver-grey aromatic shrub with tiny yellow flowers and the incomparable scent of rain on desert. Covers millions of acres across Nevada. Essential habitat for sage grouse, pronghorn, pygmy rabbit, and hundreds of specialist insects. The smell of sagebrush defines the West.

flowers.name: Desert Paintbrush
flowers.habitat: Desert washes, sagebrush steppe, dry slopes
flowers.wildlife: Critical hummingbird nectar source in desert. Also visited by hummingbird hawk-moths.
flowers.description: Brilliant orange-red bracts (modified leaves) that appear to dip a brush in orange paint. Semi-parasitic on the roots of nearby plants, making it difficult to transplant. One of the most spectacular desert wildflowers. Hummingbirds follow the bloom north as seasons progress.

flowers.name: Showy Milkweed
flowers.wildlife: Critical Monarch butterfly host plant in the West. Major nectar source for dozens of native bee species.
flowers.description: Large spherical clusters of fragrant pink-purple star-shaped flowers on substantial plants. The primary western milkweed species supporting Monarch butterfly populations. Spreads by rhizomes and self-seeds. Silky seed pods burst in fall releasing seeds on silk parachutes.

flowers.name: Desert Five-Spot
flowers.wildlife: Native desert bee forage. Blooms in conjunction with other Mojave spring ephemerals.
flowers.description: Perfect bowl-shaped pink flowers each petal with a dark wine-red spot at the base — one of the Mojave's most exquisite spring ephemerals. After winter rains, carpets entire desert washes. Lasts only until heat arrives. A desert wildflower garden treasure.

flowers.name: Prickly Pear Cactus
flowers.wildlife: Fruit (tunas) eaten by coyotes, foxes, birds, desert tortoises. Nesting site for cactus wrens.
flowers.description: Large waxy yellow flowers (sometimes pink or red) blooming from the edges of flat blue-green pads. The most cold-hardy native cactus — grows across the Great Basin and high desert. Nutritious red-purple fruit edible and prized. Spines are serious — plant away from walkways.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Syringa (Mock Orange)
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full entry.
flowers.description: Idaho's intensely fragrant state flower — white four-petaled flowers with a sweet citrus-orange scent discovered by Meriwether Lewis.

flowers.name: Mock Orange (Syringa)
flowers.wildlife: Important pollinator nectar source. Dense shrubs provide nesting cover for many birds.
flowers.description: Pure white four-petaled flowers with an intoxicating fragrance reminiscent of orange blossoms. Discovered by Meriwether Lewis in Idaho's Clearwater River canyon. Drought tolerant once established. Can reach 10 feet. The scent on a summer evening is unforgettable.

flowers.name: Camas
flowers.habitat: Wet meadows, valley bottoms, stream edges
flowers.wildlife: Major bumblebee forage. The Camas Prairie in Idaho is named for the incredible historical density of this plant.
flowers.description: Blue flower spikes that once turned Idaho's Camas Prairie blue for miles. The bulbs sustained the Nez Perce people through harsh winters and were a primary trade commodity. Now restored in prairie preserves. Mass plantings create stunning effects.

flowers.name: Balsamroot
flowers.habitat: Dry hillsides, sagebrush steppe, open pine forest
flowers.wildlife: Seeds eaten by birds and small mammals. Browsed by deer and pronghorn. Root-feeding beetles are specialists.
flowers.description: Large bright yellow sunflower-like flowers above big silver-green arrow-shaped leaves. Turns entire hillsides golden in spring. One of the iconic wildflowers of the Intermountain West. The massive taproot makes transplanting difficult — start from seed. Very long-lived.

flowers.name: Bitterbrush
flowers.habitat: Dry slopes, sagebrush steppe, ponderosa pine forest
flowers.wildlife: Critical winter browse for mule deer and pronghorn. Nitrogen fixer. Quail and grouse eat seeds.
flowers.description: Fragrant yellow five-petaled flowers on a sprawling drought-tolerant shrub. One of the most ecologically important shrubs of the Intermountain West — a critical food source for mule deer and pronghorn, especially in winter. Fixes nitrogen. A keystone species of the sagebrush ecosystem.

flowers.name: Rocky Mountain Iris
flowers.wildlife: Visited by sphinx moths and long-tongued bees. Specialist iris bees collect pollen.
flowers.description: Elegant pale blue-violet iris flowers with darker veining, growing in wet mountain meadows. One of the most beautiful mountain wildflowers. Forms dense colonies. Toxic if eaten — keeps deer and livestock from overgrazing wet meadows. Stunning when naturalized around ponds and streams.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Bitterroot
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full entry.
flowers.description: Montana's state flower — stunning multi-petaled pink flowers emerging from bare rocky ground. A symbol of resilience — survives years of drought and reanimates.

flowers.name: Bitterroot
flowers.habitat: Rocky slopes, gravelly ridges, dry exposed ground
flowers.wildlife: Native bee pollen source. Seeds dispersed by ants.
flowers.description: Montana's state flower — one of the most beautiful wildflowers in North America. Multi-petaled satiny pink flowers (up to 2 inches across) emerge from bare rocky ground in spring after the leaves have died back. Incredibly drought resistant — dried specimens kept as museum curiosities have been rehydrated and bloomed. Named Lewisia for Meriwether Lewis.

flowers.name: Blanket Flower (Native)
flowers.wildlife: Major native bee nectar and pollen source. Supports 30+ bee species. Goldfinches eat seeds.
flowers.description: Bold red-orange ray petals tipped with yellow around a maroon-red center disc. The parent species of most cultivated Gaillardia. Long-blooming, drought-tolerant native of Montana's prairies and slopes. Self-seeds prolifically. One of the most reliable and showy native perennials.

flowers.name: Prairie Smoke
flowers.habitat: Dry prairies, open slopes, rocky ridges
flowers.wildlife: Early bee forage. Seeds dispersed by wind — feathery plumes very effective.
flowers.description: Three nodding pink-red bell-shaped flowers per stem, but the show really starts after bloom — as seeds develop, long feathery pink-purple plumes create the effect of wisps of smoke rising from the prairie. One of the most distinctive and beautiful native plants for texture and movement.

flowers.name: Shooting Star
flowers.wildlife: Buzz-pollinated by bumblebees — the unique flower shape forces bees to vibrate pollen loose.
flowers.description: Remarkable flowers that look like tiny magenta shooting stars or darts — swept-back petals and a protruding pointed dark beak. Grows in moist mountain meadows. Buzz-pollinated by bumblebees which vibrate the anthers at the right frequency. Dies back completely in summer. Unforgettable.

flowers.name: Rocky Mountain Columbine
flowers.habitat: Mountain meadows, rocky slopes, aspen groves
flowers.wildlife: Hummingbird nectar plant. Long-tongued bumblebees reach nectar. Hawkmoths pollinate at night.
flowers.description: Colorado's state flower — also abundant across Montana's mountains. Large blue-and-white two-toned flowers with long nectar spurs on a delicate many-branched plant. One of North America's most beautiful wildflowers. Self-seeds readily in gardens. Hybridizes with other columbines.
